newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Ousted Cambodian Prince main question in talks.
newsitem.headline: Ousted Cambodian Prince main question in talks.

text.p: Cambodian strongman Hun Sen and an ASEAN mediation team agreed on Saturday on the need to end conflict and hold elections but appeared inconclusive on a role for ousted Prince Norodom Ranariddh.

The Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) delegation, led by Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas, said it had raised the question of Ranariddh's future role in Cambodian politics during its nearly three hours of talks with Hun Sen.
"Of course we talked about Prince Ranariddh's role, both now and in the future elections," Alatas told a news conference after the talks.
But Alatas said Hun Sen's position on the prince was equivocal.
"It was not such a straightforward position that we got, it was not black or white," Alatas said.
Second Prime Minister Hun Sen ousted his senior co-premier and coalition partner, Prince Norodom Ranariddh, on July 6 after two days of battles in Phnom Penh.

Alatas said the ASEAN mission stressed that next year's election, which Hun Sen has repeatedly said he will hold, would be meaningless unless all political players could take part freely. He said Hun Sen agreed with that position.
"He agreed with us that the general elections in May would have no meaning unless participated in by all political forces, and all political parties, freely," Alatas said.
Ranariddh left Cambodia shortly before his ouster and has since called from abroad for opposition to his former coalition partner, Hun Sen.
Hun Sen has said the prince was free to go home but he would have to face trial for his illegal negotiations with the outlawed Khmer Rouge guerrilla group and for alleged weapons smuggling.
Hun Sen suggested on Saturday that Ranariddh should not come back to Cambodia as to do so could lead to conflict.
"Whether Ranariddh should return or not return I don't know," Hun Sen told reporters after his talks with the ASEAN team.
But he went on to cite Alatas and others as saying that Ranariddh's return could raise tension and prolong conflict in Cambodia.
Alatas declined to give further details of the discussion with Hun Sen concerning the ousted prince, saying the ASEAN envoys had to consult the prince first.
Hun Sen initially rejected all offers of mediation in Cambodia's crisis and slammed outside interference.

Two weeks ago he dismissed an ASEAN offer when Alatas and his two colleagues, foreign ministers Prachuab Chaiyasan of Thailand and Domingo Siazon of the Philippines, visited Phnom Penh. He later agreed to meet the envoys again.
Alatas said both sides had agreed on the need to end the conflict in Cambodia and Hun Sen asked the envoys to convey that message to Ranariddh.
The ASEAN envoys also suggested that Hun Sen issue a clear guarantee for the safety of opposition politicians who fled abroad after the prince's ouster.

Hun Sen presented the envoys with an aide memoire in which he encouraged opposition politicians to return and said the government would reinstate royalist soldiers who returned to the government side with the exception of several top commanders.
Saturday's aide memoire also called on Ranariddh to cease his fight against the government and stop collaborating with the Khmer Rouge guerrilla group.
Ranariddh was negotiating with the Khmer Rouge before his ouster but has since denied links with the rebels.
The Khmer Rouge, who purged their notorious leader Pol Pot last week, have said they support Ranariddh and have vowed to unite with all anti-Hun Sen forces and "destroy" his government.

A Khmer Rouge military commander told the Far Eastern Economic Review in a report published on Thursday that Pol Pot, responsible for the death of more than a million people during his 1975-79 rule, was targeted because of his opposition to an alliance with the royalists.
